scope: Fresh profiling and ranked optimization targets. No production changes and no new solver speedup claim.

method.cpu: Three full-file CPU captures per engine, alternating engine order; 24 workers, all 25 isolates, 1000 us samples.
method.native: One full-file single-worker raw-PC capture per engine at 250 us with same-process native disassembly.
method.phases: Isolated copies add thread CPU and monotonic wall clocks around chunk read/parse, kernel setup, consume and result export, plus lifecycle marks. Production hot-loop source and Wasm bytes are unchanged.
method.phaseAggregation: One warm-up per case is excluded from the phase analysis, matching the paired controls. Never add concurrent wall spans as whole-process elapsed time. Consume includes read and parse.
method.tier: V8 GetOptimizationStatus observed before and after each Node parser call in a diagnostic copy only; --allow-natives-syntax does not ship. No forced optimization. Status bits checked in the local Node 26.12.0 source, runtime.h:1117 and runtime-test.cc:895.
limitations: Raw sample percentages are not elapsed-time components or predicted speedups. CPU profiles include main-thread idle.
Single-worker native shares are not the 24-worker distribution. PC sampling does not identify cache misses, branch misses or individual instruction latency.
Phase probes add measured overhead and can perturb tier timing. Early/steady comparisons diagnose costs, not a candidate speedup.
threadCpuUsage is quantized; aggregate many chunks. It excludes background compiler threads. Pending optimization status does not distinguish queue wait from active compilation.
Tier status at call boundaries does not identify on-stack replacement within a call, or measure compiler CPU.
12/24-worker comparisons are five-round screens and are not sufficient to change production defaults.
Hardware/software perf counters remain unavailable under perf_event_paranoid=4; system settings unchanged.
Short-phase attribution is approximate: the 12-worker read CPU estimate reaches 107% of read wall spans. Do not treat phase ratios as exact blocked-time accounting.

nodeNative.loopAttributionCaveat: Line 167 has 798/27668 parser ticks here (2.88%), including tagged comparisons, stack reloads and cursor shifts. Its 8.5-9.6% multiworker line attribution does not prove a branch bottleneck.

wasmNative.interpretation: Verified 15 actual SIMD station-head load/equality blocks in fresh disassembly. The bucket pointer supplies the next key-load address. This proves a dependency, not its hardware stall cost.

rankedTargets.name: Hash-indexed short-key side table with dense statistics
rankedTargets.evidence: 15 short-key load/equality blocks take 4105/9835 optimized parser ticks (41.74%, 31.00% of all single-worker ticks). Native code has hash -> bucket pointer -> key address -> SIMD equality.
rankedTargets.experiment: Keep dense Station aggregates and existing bucket pointers. Add a 16-byte canonical short-key entry indexed directly by the hash slot, so key validation can load independently of the bucket pointer. Preserve complete 16-byte equality, collision fallback, resets and retuning.
rankedTargets.differenceFromRejected: b6a3e22 only rescheduled dependent loads and grew native code to 17444 bytes without a gain. 583395f moved BOTH stats and keys into sparse 32-byte slots and lost on the earlier CPU. This experiment keeps writes dense and changes only the key-address dependency.
rankedTargets.risk: The new 512 KiB key table increases footprint and retune/reset work. The sample share is not a predicted saving. Native ordering and real timings decide.

rankedTargets.name: Shorten cold parsing and normal tier-up
rankedTargets.evidence: At 24 workers, first-eight-chunk parser CPU is 26.54 ns/logical byte versus 1.44 after chunk 2048 in the five-run phase diagnostic. A separate three-run tier diagnostic finds 3.71% of bytes but 8.22% of parser thread CPU in calls without TurboFan attached at both boundaries; some are in baseline code with concurrent optimization pending.
rankedTargets.experiment: First compare normal earlier TurboFan/OSR thresholds and V8 background pool widths against the current defaults. Then, independently, specialize the default two-lane parser entry and outline cold miss work if native/bytecode evidence shows a smaller compilation job. Keep complete CLI startup in every benchmark; no V8 intrinsics in production.
rankedTargets.differenceFromRejected: Prior eager-tier experiments targeted Wasm; this targets observed JavaScript lower-tier work. Earlier additive-feedback controls did not establish a compiler cause and are not treated as proof here.
rankedTargets.risk: Pending optimization includes queueing and compilation; no compiler CPU claim. Earlier compilation can use weaker feedback or compete for cores. Probes themselves perturb tier timing, so only uninstrumented confirmations count.

rankedTargets.name: Compact packed-prediction plus exact-head cache
rankedTargets.evidence: The exact head comparison is 10.21-10.56% of all 24-worker samples and 3498/27668 native parser ticks. The current record-head load depends on the ID fetched from the predictor.
rankedTargets.experiment: Test an eight-byte predictor entry containing the current packed ID/length and the exact first four name bytes. Load both from the hash-derived slot, removing the ID-dependent head load. Keep tail/middle/full-name and delimiter validation plus the authoritative fallback.
rankedTargets.differenceFromRejected: 89f8830 copied head, tail and middle into a 16-byte entry (512 KiB) and lost. This is a bounded revisit using only two words (256 KiB), with the retained packed metadata and current equality helper; it is not a claim that the old layout now wins.
rankedTargets.risk: Doubles the current 128 KiB cache, so cache footprint may outweigh the removed dependency. Confirm both hot lanes actually lose the record-head load before benchmark confirmation.

deprioritized: Read calls are approximately 96% CPU time in the first phase capture batch. Async IO cannot hide much blocked read time in this cached-file workload. A copy-avoidance redesign is a different hypothesis; the prior mmap experiment lost.
Wasm kernel compile/instantiate/reset averages about 1-2 ms per worker; sharing its compilation again is not a leading target.
24-worker consume completion spread is about 0.1-0.2 ms for Node and usually 0.3 ms for Wasm. The existing chunk queue already controls the end tail well.
Merge takes about 3 ms for Node and 5 ms for Wasm, formatting below 1 ms. GC remains below 0.6% of CPU samples. These are small targets.
The five-round 12/24 control timings are effectively tied (Node 1.060/1.062 s, Wasm 0.474/0.476 s). Earlier worker-count screens were inconsistent, so defaults remain unchanged.
Do not repeat generic attributes, comparison spellings or the rejected three-lane key staging under a new label.
No theoretical optimum is established, and these profiles do not demonstrate a large achievable speedup.
